errors.meaning: The acting user is the person who bought the goods.
errors.note: Another member of staff receives them. In a school with one storekeeper who also does the buying, this is an open question the use case raises and does not answer (BR-5, A4, OQ-1).

errors.meaning: A quantity was entered in a different unit from the item's.
errors.note: It could not be added to the balance without conversion (BR-9).

errors.meaning: Less arrived than was approved and no reason was given.
errors.note: A request part-filled is not a request completed (BR-8).

errors.written: The receipt is recorded and flagged.
errors.note: It may indicate a reimbursement is being sought, and one needs approval before it is paid (BR-4, E7).

planningRules.rule: Record what arrived, never what was approved. The two are allowed to differ and the difference is the point — an approved quantity copied into the received column is a shortfall assumed away and an item the school still does not have (BR-8, E4).

Never receive goods the acting user bought. It is the cheapest control in the module against one person requesting, taking the cash, purchasing and returning the receipt, and it is worth saying why rather than reading as an obstruction (BR-5, E1, A4).
Never proceed without the supplier receipt. The whole settlement rests on it, and a receipt promised later is a settlement against a figure nobody can check (BR-2, E2).

Check the unit against the item before the number. Ten of something counted in reams and ten counted in boxes add differently to the same balance, and the delivery note rarely uses the store's unit (BR-9, E3).

Say that the balance has not moved yet. The goods are on the shelf and the system does not show them until Accounts post the settlement — that is deliberate, because the money and the stock move together or neither does (BR-3, BR-11, E6).
Name the difference against the advance either way. Over means somebody is owed money and it needs approval before it is paid; under means cash is in a pocket until it is recorded back (BR-4, E7).
branch_id comes from $session.

reversal.statement: A receipt is never deleted. A wrong one is corrected by a stock adjustment, which carries its own reason and its own approval (BR-10, E10, A6) — so the record shows both what was recorded and what corrected it.

intent.name: stock.advance.settle
intent.summary: Post the settlement: the amount to the ledger and the stock onto the shelf, together or not at all.

routesHere.gloss: settle the advance for the marker request

request.gloss: just post it to the ledger, stock later

routesElsewhere.note: Both halves are recorded together or not at all. A voucher records an amount, while stock needs to know that ten reams arrived — without the second half the books are clean and the inventory never moves (BR-3, BR-11, E6).

request.text: bacha hua paisa bhi likh dein
request.gloss: record the unspent cash too

routesElsewhere.note: The cash handed back is its own record, because it is money physically returned rather than an accounting entry (BR-4).

steps.note: One step with two halves. The amount posts to the ledger and the stock balance rises by what arrived — a settled advance with no stock increase is the failure this is built to prevent (BR-11).

plan.onFailure: Stop and report. Where either half fails the whole settlement is rolled back and nothing is recorded — the advance stays outstanding and the goods stay unrecorded on the shelf (E6).
plan.atomicity: One atomic act: the ledger posting, the stock increase, and the advance ceasing to be an amount owed back. **The advance becomes an expense at this moment and not before** (BR-6, E9). Where the receipt exceeded the advance the settlement waits for a reimbursement approval rather than paying the difference (BR-4, E7).

planningRules.rule: Never post one half without the other. The amount and the stock move together or neither does — this is the single most consequential rule in the module, because the books look right either way and the shelf does not (BR-3, BR-11, E6).

Say that the expense happens here. Until this moment the money was an amount owed back; the ledger entry that turns it into a cost is this one, and posting it earlier is the error the module names as most likely (BR-6, E9).
Never settle past a difference. Cash short of the advance is still in somebody's pocket until it is recorded back, and cash over it is not paid until a reimbursement is approved (BR-4, E7).
Report a rolled-back settlement as nothing recorded. The advance is still outstanding and the goods are still on the shelf unrecorded — both true and neither visible unless it is said (E6).
Say which items are still short. Where less arrived than was approved, settling closes the money and leaves the shortage; the item goes back on the next round (BR-8).

planningRules.rule: Never write the reason. Somebody is being told they will not be repaid money they spent, and "not approved" is not an answer that anybody can act on next time (BR-4, A5).
Say that the goods stay. Refusing the reimbursement does not send anything back — what arrived was recorded as arriving and stays in stock, so the school keeps the extra and does not pay for it (E5).
Name who is out of pocket and by how much. Nothing else in the system tracks it, and the person who bought the school's supplies is the one carrying it (BR-4).
branch_id comes from $session.

reversal.statement: The decision can be taken the other way afterwards — the receipt goes back to Received rather than to a terminal state, so an approval can still follow (A5, A2).

steps.note: Their words, and the purchaser reads them (PR-1).

resolvedPlans.outcome: Report the refusal and then the two things it leaves standing: the extra boxes are in stock and stay there, so the school keeps goods it has not paid for; and Imran Sultan is PKR 250 down with nothing else in the system tracking it. The decision can still be taken the other way — this does not close the receipt permanently.
